name: Yankton Sioux Tribe
land_summary: The Yankton Sioux Tribe, the Ihanktonwan, once held a wide territory between the Missouri, James and Big Sioux rivers. In a treaty signed April 19, 1858, the Yankton ceded more than 11 million acres and kept a reservation of about 400,000 acres along the Missouri in what is now Charles Mix County, South Dakota. Allotment came next: by 1891 about 262,000 acres had been divided into individual allotments. In 1892 the tribe agreed to sell roughly 168,000 unallotted acres to the United States for $600,000, and Congress ratified the sale in 1894. Over the next decades many allotments passed out of Native hands. The Fort Randall Dam project took 2,851.40 acres on the reservation's western edge, compensated further by Congress in 2002. In 1998 the U.S. Supreme Court held that the 1894 sale diminished the reservation, and later federal rulings found that the reservation still exists on its remaining trust and agency lands, roughly 37,000 acres. The tribal offices are in Wagner.

timeline.event: By the treaty of April 19, signed in Washington, the Yankton cede more than 11 million acres and keep a reservation of about 400,000 acres on the Missouri River.
The treaty is ratified on February 16, and the Yankton Agency is set up on the Missouri River near Greenwood.
Allotment under the Dawes Act and an 1891 Act divides about 262,000 acres into individual allotments.
Congress ratifies, on August 15, the tribe's 1892 agreement to sell about 168,000 acres of unallotted land for $600,000.
In South Dakota v. Yankton Sioux Tribe, the U.S. Supreme Court holds that the 1894 sale diminished the reservation and puts the ceded lands under state jurisdiction.
Congress finds that 2,851.40 acres of Yankton land were taken for the Fort Randall Dam and Reservoir and approves added compensation.
A federal district court rules that the reservation was diminished but not disestablished, a finding the Eighth Circuit later upholds for trust and agency lands.

notes: yanktonsiouxtribe.net loads, but its homepage has only a CodeRED alert and an office address in Wagner, and no history pages were found. That is why homelands is null. 'Wagner' comes from the nation's site. There is no nation figure for current acreage, and the sources disagree. SD Tribal Relations says 36,741 trust acres. SD State Archives says about 40,000, which as a second agency of the same state government does not count as independent. ICT/AP (2008) gives about 37,585 acres for the remaining reservation, and the Eighth Circuit's parcel figures add up to about 37,410. The summary says 'roughly 37,000.' The survey figure of 430,405 acres for the 1858 reservation (it appears only in the court opinions) was left out. The Yankton Agency's founding in 1859 is single-sourced (SD Archives); the 1859 entry rests on the ratification date. 'Disputed' is set to true because the reservation's extent has been litigated for decades and the Eighth Circuit left the status of Indian-owned fee lands open. The 1929 return of agency lands, the 1963 IRA constitution and the 1930 figure of 43,358 acres still in allotments were left out as single-sourced. The 2007 entry's date comes from ICT's report on Judge Piersol's ruling. The 2010 Eighth Circuit opinion reviews that ruling.
